why: Evidence from the 120s / 9785-request load test: canary 1.1 took 2411 requests and returned 0 5xx (0.00% err), same as stable's 0 5xx over 7374 requests. Overall latency is at parity: canary p50/p95/p99 = 34/93/105ms vs stable 34/94/104ms. Per-endpoint parity holds too: /browse 22/27 (p50/p95) on both; /search 47/59/61 identical on both; /checkout 82/104/107 vs stable 81/103/105, i.e. within 1-2ms. The time-series shows no degradation trend and no errors in any window: canary p95 92, 92, 93, 96 vs stable 94, 94, 95, 92 - the final-window 96 vs 92 is a 4ms gap on a single pod, inside normal noise. The one real anomaly is canary /browse p99 = 77ms vs stable 28ms. Judgement: this is not a blocker, because /browse p50 and p95 are identical to stable (22/27ms), so the effect is confined to under ~5% of /browse requests, and 77ms absolute is still well below what /checkout serves at p50 (82ms) on both versions; a single canary pod with 1200 requests is also the most likely place to see warmup/JIT or scheduling tail outliers. Judgement: no customer-visible harm is evident - zero errors and equal p95 everywhere - so blocking the release is not justified. Promote, but watch /browse p99 after the canary scales to 100%: if the tail stays elevated with 4 pods and full traffic, that rules out single-pod warmup noise and should trigger a rollback.
